solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cheap stuff in pile, first in sale to go

indicators.note: the letter picked is told to go, that is, be removed from the word for pile

parts.note: a stack is a pile of things

indicators.note: the first letter in the word sale is the one picked

explanation.surface: Someone browsing a heap of bargains at the start of a sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Tack, as in tacky, is shoddy or tasteless goods; Chambers glosses it as rubbish or cheap stuff.

clue.text: Like some in Lords, having spoken with a small degree of heat to start with

indicators.note: says the heat piece comes first, ahead of the word for spoken

parts.note: temp is the short form of temperature, a degree of heat
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: A peer making a heated speech in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords has Lords Spiritual (bishops) and Lords Temporal (the lay peers).
explanation.definitionFit: The lay members of the House of Lords are called the Lords Temporal, as opposed to the bishops.

clue.text: Previously king in court would want old instrumental piece

indicators.note: the time word and the king are placed inside the court abbreviation

parts.note: once means at some previous time
R is for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch holding court calls for an old piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would want' just says the O is wanted at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A concerto is a musical work for a solo instrument and orchestra, so an instrumental piece.

clue.text: Modern aid's worked out what letters of anagram could be

definitions.text: what letters of anagram could be

indicators.note: letters that are worked out are rearranged until something new emerges

explanation.surface: A modern aid has solved a puzzle, an anagram perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters of an anagram are shuffled into a random order, which is the point of the clue type.

clue.text: Tree with less on top? No top at all!

indicators.note: no top means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: someone with less hair on top is balder

explanation.surface: A jokey line about a tree with thinning foliage, and then none at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less on top' reads as hair, so BALDER; 'No top' drops its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The alder is a tree of the birch family, common by rivers.

clue.text: Spooner's desire, girl becoming the epitome of dullness

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the first sounds of words, so the opening sounds of the two pieces trade places

parts.note: a wish is a desire
a daughter is a girl

explanation.surface: Someone longing for a girl to turn into something dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The swap is by sound: W and D trade places, giving words spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as dull as dishwater' makes it the stock example of tedium.

clue.text: Front of cafe I admire built badly, strange to say

indicators.note: something built badly is put together wrongly, so these letters are rearranged
picks the opening letter of the word cafe

explanation.surface: Someone admires a shoddily built cafe frontage.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means wonderful to relate, used for something remarkable or strange to mention.

clue.text: Understand wise words and oscillate

parts.note: to see is to understand, as in 'I see'
a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: A wavering person who takes in some wisdom then swings between views.
explanation.definitionFit: To seesaw is to move back and forth or up and down, alternating like a swinging plank.

clue.text: Hate exam after getting low grades

indicators.note: says the exam piece follows the grades piece

parts.note: D and E are low grades in an exam
a test is an exam

explanation.surface: A student loathes exams after getting poor marks.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to loathe it intensely, a strong form of the verb.

clue.text: Chap's by a road constructing top of building

parts.note: a chap is a man, with the possessive s kept

explanation.surface: A man by the roadside putting up the top of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A mansard is a roof with two slopes on each side, forming the top storey of a building.

clue.text: Like a sort of movement that goes back in time?

definitions.text: Like a sort of movement that goes back in time?

parts.words: Like a sort of movement that goes back in time?
parts.note: a clock's hands moving backwards would seem to turn back time, and that direction of rotation is the sense wanted

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a movement that travels backwards through time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back in time' suggests time travel; it is just a clock run in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning against the direction of a clock's hands is the rotation that would wind time backwards.

clue.text: Treacherous type, very French, about to ensnare writer

indicators.note: the reversed word traps the writer piece inside it
turning about means the French word is written backwards

parts.note: tres is French for very
a pen is a writer, something to write with

explanation.surface: A treacherous Frenchman about to trap an author.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent, from the snake in Eden, stands for a sly or treacherous person.

clue.text: Put an end to careless action on cricket field?

definitions.meaning: to topple or abolish, as a government or regime
in cricket, a throw from a fielder that misses the stumps and lets the batsmen take extra runs

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder's sloppy throw finishes a match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a wild throw past the wicket lets the batsmen run more, and the extra runs carry the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to topple a ruler; the noun is a cricket fielder's wayward throw giving away runs.

clue.text: Money needed for memorial

definitions.meaning: slang for cash, as in 'where there's muck there's...'
an engraved metal plaque set in a church floor or wall to commemorate someone

explanation.surface: Funds must be raised to pay for a memorial.
explanation.definitionFit: It is British slang for cash, and also a commemorative engraved plate in a church.

clue.text: Rite actually interpreted in an eloquent manner

indicators.note: interpreting a text recasts it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ritual is explained in fluent, well-chosen words.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking articulately means expressing yourself clearly and fluently, as an eloquent speaker does.

clue.text: Giving up in turn after renting property

indicators.note: says the turn piece follows the renting piece

parts.note: letting is renting out property
a go is a turn, as in 'your go'

explanation.surface: A landlord gives up their turn after letting out a property.
explanation.definitionFit: Releasing something or abandoning it, ceasing to grip it, is giving it up.

clue.text: Above river supply rope for support?

indicators.note: in a down entry, the supply piece sits on top of the river piece

parts.note: the mains is the public supply of water, gas or electricity
the Tay is a river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A water supply drawn from upriver, with a rope as backup.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the literal ship's rope also means a chief support.
explanation.definitionFit: On a sailing ship it is the stay holding up the mainmast, hence figuratively a chief support.

clue.text: One to argue back, boy ending in trouble kept in

indicators.note: the boy and the letter are held inside the word for back

parts.note: the rear is the back
a son is a boy

indicators.note: picks the closing letter of the word trouble

explanation.surface: A boy who argues back ends up kept in after school for trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'argue back' looks like a phrase, but 'back' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reasons is a person who argues logically, making a case step by step.

clue.text: Sort of student job to jar — notice university intervening

parts.note: a post is a job

indicators.note: the notice and university pieces come between letters of the word for jar

parts.note: to grate is to jar, as on the nerves
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: A student's job involves a jar, with a university notice in between.
explanation.definitionFit: A student studying after a first degree, for a master's or doctorate, is one kind of student.

clue.text: Cat in church, see, hiding in books there?

indicators.note: the church and see pieces are hidden away inside the books piece

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
CE is the Church of England
lo is an old word for look or see

explanation.surface: A cat in church, hiding among the books there.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of Central and South America.

clue.text: Piece of music with a beat bigger than usual coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to tan is to beat, as in 'tan someone's hide'
OS is outsize, the label on large clothes

explanation.surface: A musical piece played with a heavier beat than usual is coming up.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a classical composition, usually in several movements for one or two instruments.

clue.text: Sound from King Charles — where was he hiding?

parts.note: CR is Carolus Rex, Charles the king
Charles II hid in an oak tree after the Battle of Worcester

explanation.surface: A noise from King Charles, and a question about his hiding place.
explanation.walkthrough: After losing the Battle of Worcester (1651), Charles II hid in an oak tree at Boscobel, the Royal Oak of pub names.
explanation.definitionFit: A croak is a hoarse sound, like a frog's call or a husky voice.

clue.text: Home boy returning without money? They should not be blamed

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside: the reversed boy goes around the money
the boy word is written backwards

parts.note: a son is a boy
a cent is a coin, a unit of money

explanation.surface: A boy comes home broke, but nobody is at fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without money' reads as broke, but 'without' is the old sense of outside, a container signal; 'returning' turns the boy round.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who are blameless, guiltless of any wrong, are the innocent ones.

clue.text: Man's heading off when it's time to retire

indicators.note: the first letter of the piece goes, cutting off its head

parts.note: a man is a chess piece such as a knight; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: A man sets off home when it's bedtime.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess the pieces are called men. 'heading off' sounds like leaving, but it means losing the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring here means going to bed, which people do after dark.

clue.text: Blank space in print is most important

definitions.meaning: in typesetting, the space between lines of type, once made with strips of lead
chief or foremost, as in a top actor

explanation.surface: A printer insists that white space is the key element.
explanation.definitionFit: Typesetters' name for spacing between lines, from lead strips, also means principal or foremost.

clue.text: Time in good English town gets one indulging

indicators.note: the time letter goes inside the town

parts.note: Luton is a town in Bedfordshire, England

explanation.surface: Spending time in a pleasant English town turns one self-indulgent.
explanation.definitionFit: A greedy person who indulges in food or drink to excess is a classic overindulger.

clue.text: Way to take stuff to market

definitions.text: Way to take stuff to market

parts.words: Way to take stuff to market
parts.note: a road or route along which merchants carry goods for sale

explanation.surface: A road for carrying goods to the market.
explanation.definitionFit: A path used by merchants to carry goods for sale, like the Silk Road.

clue.text: Writer Dorothy avoiding extremes as a philosopher

indicators.note: the outermost letters of the surname are left out

parts.note: Dorothy L. Sayers wrote the Lord Peter Wimsey detective novels

explanation.surface: A novelist steers a moderate course, like a philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: A. J. Ayer was the British philosopher who wrote Language, Truth and Logic.
